<problem_statement><![CDATA[Let $ABC$ be a triangle. Points $D$, $E$, and $F$ lie on sides $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$, respectively, such that
\[
\angle AFE = \angle BDF = \angle CED.
\]
Let $O_A$, $O_B$, and $O_C$ be the circumcenters of triangles $AFE$, $BDF$, and $CED$, respectively. Let $M$, $N$, and $O$ be the circumcenters of triangles $ABC$, $DEF$, and $O_A O_B O_C$, respectively. Prove that $OM = ON$.]]></problem_statement>

<reference_solution><![CDATA[Claim 1. We have $\triangle ABC\sim\triangle EFD\sim \triangle O_AO_BO_C$. 
Proof. The given angle condition implies that $DE$ is tangent to $(AFE)$, so $\angle DEF = \angle EAF = \angle CAB$. Similarly, $\angle EFD = \angle ABC$, so 
\[\triangle ABC\sim \triangle EFD.\] 
Now by Miquel's theorem, the three circles $(AFE)$, $(BDF)$, and $(CED)$ meet at a point $P$. Note that $O_BO_A$ and $O_BO_C$ are the perpendicular bisectors of $PF$ and $PD$ respectively. Then $\angle O_AO_BO_C = \frac{1}{2}\angle FO_BD = \angle FBD = \angle ABC$. Similarly, $\angle O_BO_CO_A = \angle BCA$ so 
\[\triangle O_AO_BO_C\sim \triangle ABC.\]

Claim 2. $P$ is the center of a spiral similarity between $\triangle ABC$, $\triangle EFD$, and $\triangle O_AO_BO_C$.
Proof. From Claim 1, it suffices to show $\triangle PAB\sim \triangle PEF\sim \triangle PO_AO_B$. From cyclic quadrilateral $PEAF$, we have $\angle PAB = \angle PEF$. Also, $\angle PO_AO_B = \frac{1}{2}\angle PO_AF = \angle PEF$, so 
\[\angle PAB = \angle PEF = \angle PO_AO_B.\]
Since $EF$ is tangent to $(PBF)$, we have $\angle PBA = \angle PFE$. Also, $\angle PO_BO_A = \frac{1}{2}\angle PO_BF = \angle PBA$, so 
\[\angle PBA = \angle PFE = \angle PO_BO_A.\]

Adding in the circumcenters, $P$ is the center of a spiral similarity between $ABCM$, $EFDN$, and $O_AO_BO_CO$. As spiral similarities come in pairs, $P$ is also the center of spiral similarity from $\triangle AEO_A$ to $\triangle MNO$. As $O_AA = O_AE$, we have $OM = ON$.]]></reference_solution>

<candidate_solution><![CDATA[We prove the statement by using a complex model.  
Let the circumcircle of \(ABC\) be the unit circle and place its centre \(M\) at the origin \(0\).  
Write the vertices as complex numbers \(a,b,c\) with \(|a|=|b|=|c|=1\).  
The points on the sides are written as  

\[
f=(1-\lambda)a+\lambda b,\qquad 
e=(1-\mu)c+\mu a,\qquad 
d=(1-\nu)b+\nu c\qquad (\lambda,\mu,\nu\in\mathbb R).
\]

The common angle is denoted \(\omega\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Miquel point and a spiral similarity

The circles \(\omega_A=(AEF)\), \(\omega_B=(BFD)\), \(\omega_C=(CDE)\) have a second
common point \(X\) (Miquel point).  
Because \(\angle AFE=\omega\), the inscribed angle in \(\omega_A\) over chord \(AE\)
is \(\omega\); hence  

\[
\angle AXE=\omega. \tag{1}
\]

Analogously  

\[
\angle BXF=\omega,\qquad \angle CXD=\omega. \tag{2}
\]

From the cyclic quadrilaterals we obtain  

\[
\angle XAB=\angle XEF \qquad(\text{since }A,F,B\text{ collinear}), \tag{3}
\]
\[
\angle XBA=\angle XDF. \tag{4}
\]

A similar chase using the three circles shows that  

\[
\angle XDF=\angle XAE. \tag{5}
\]

Indeed, in \(\omega_B\) we have \(\angle XDF=\angle XBF\) (same chord \(XF\));
in \(\omega_A\) \(\angle XAE=\angle XFE\); and equality of the arcs
\(AE=BF=CD=2\omega\) forces \(\angle XFE=\angle XDF\), which together with
(4) and (5) gives \(\angle XBA=\angle XFE\).
Thus triangles \(XAB\) and \(XEF\) have two equal angles and are
similar. Consequently  

\[
\frac{XA}{XE}=\frac{XB}{XF}=:\rho^{-1} \quad\text{(so }XE=\rho\,XA,\;XF=\rho\,XB\text{)}. \tag{6}
\]

Cyclic permutations yield the same ratio \(\rho\) for the other vertices.
Hence \(X\) is the centre of a **direct similarity** with rotation \(\omega\)
and ratio \(\rho\) that sends \(A\mapsto E\), \(B\mapsto F\), \(C\mapsto D\).
Therefore  

\[
E-X=\rho\,R_\omega(A-X),\qquad
F-X=\rho\,R_\omega(B-X),\qquad
D-X=\rho\,R_\omega(C-X), \tag{7}
\]

where \(R_\omega\) denotes rotation through \(\omega\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  The circumcenters \(O_A,O_B,O_C\)

Consider \(\omega_A\).  Since \(X\in\omega_A\) we have \(O_AA=O_AX\); thus
\(O_A\) lies on the perpendicular bisector of \(AX\).  Writing \(J\) for a
\(90^\circ\) rotation (\(J^2=-I\)), the bisector can be parametrised as  

\[
O_A=\frac{A+X}{2}+t_A\,J(A-X) \qquad (t_A\in\mathbb R). \tag{8}
\]

The same holds for \(O_B,O_C\) with (possibly different) parameters.
Moreover, in \(\omega_A\) the chord \(AE\) subtends a *central* angle
\(2\omega\) (because the inscribed angle \(\angle AFE=\omega\)).
Using (7) we express  

\[
E-X=\rho\,R_\omega(A-X).
\]

Writing \(O_A=X+\gamma(A-X)\) with \(\gamma=\frac12+i t_A\) (the
identification comes from (8)),
the equality of the radii \(O_AA=O_AE\) becomes  

\[
|\gamma-1| = |\gamma-\rho e^{i\omega}|. \tag{9}
\]

The condition that the central angle \(\angle A O_A E\) equals \(2\omega\) is
equivalent to  

\[
\gamma-\rho e^{i\omega} = (\gamma-1)\,e^{i2\omega}. \tag{10}
\]

Solving (10) for \(\rho\) (separating real and imaginary parts) gives  

\[
\rho = \cos\omega + 2t_A\sin\omega. \tag{11}
\]

Exactly the same reasoning applied to \(\omega_B\) and \(\omega_C\) yields the
same value of \(t_A,T_B,T_C\) because the right‑hand side of (11) involves
only the common \(\rho\) and \(\omega\).
Denote this common value by \(t\).  Then

\[
\boxed{\,\gamma=\frac12+i t,\qquad \rho=\cos\omega+2t\sin\omega\,}. \tag{12}
\]

Consequently  

\[
O_A = X+\gamma(A-X),\qquad O_B = X+\gamma(B-X),\qquad O_C = X+\gamma(C-X). \tag{13}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Centres \(M,N,O\)

Let \(M\) be the circumcentre of \(ABC\) and \(N\) of \(DEF\).
The similarity (7) maps the circumcircle of \(ABC\) to that of \(DEF\);
hence  

\[
N = X+\rho\,R_\omega(M-X). \tag{14}
\]

The points \(O_A,O_B,O_C\) are obtained from \(A,B,C\) by the same
similarity \(\psi(P)=X+\gamma(P-X)\).  Therefore the circumcentre of
\(\triangle O_AO_BO_C\) is  

\[
O = \psi(M)=X+\gamma(M-X). \tag{15}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Equality \(OM=ON\)

Put \(u=M-X\).  From (15) and (14)

\[
O-M = (X+\gamma u)-(X+u)=u(\gamma-1),\qquad 
O-N = (X+\gamma u)-(X+\rho e^{i\omega}u)=u(\gamma-\rho e^{i\omega}).
\]

Because \(\gamma=\frac12+it\) has real part \(\frac12\), one checks that  
\(|\gamma-1|=|\gamma|\).  Hence  

\[
|O-M|^2 = |\gamma-1|^2|u|^2 = |\gamma|^2|u|^2.\tag{16}
\]

Now compute \(|\gamma-\rho e^{i\omega}|^2\).  Using (12),

\[
\begin{aligned}
|\gamma-\rho e^{i\omega}|^2
&= \Bigl|\,\Bigl(\tfrac12-\bigl(\cos\omega+2t\sin\omega\bigr)\cos\omega\Bigr)
   + i\Bigl(t-\bigl(\cos\omega+2t\sin\omega\bigr)\sin\omega\Bigr)\Bigr|^2\\[2mm]
&= \left(\tfrac12-\cos^2\omega-2t\sin\omega\cos\omega\right)^2
   +\left(t-\cos\omega\sin\omega-2t\sin^2\omega\right)^2\\[2mm]
&= \frac14 + t^2 \qquad\text{(after expanding and using } \sin^2+\cos^2=1\text{)}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus \(|\gamma-\rho e^{i\omega}|^2 = |\gamma|^2\).  Together with (16) we obtain  

\[
|O-M| = |O-N|.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Conclusion

\(OM\) and \(ON\) are equal, which completes the proof. ∎]]></candidate_solution>
